item.title: Trump says U.S. will halt $4 billion in annual aid to Israel and shift to selling arms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump declared Tuesday that the U.S. will end nearly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel, an unusually timed announcement on Election Day that could set up a standoff with Congress. The president said on "Fox and Friends" that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed "months ago" to stop the aid by the end of the year. "They're fine with it because they've become a very successful country," Trump said. "They don't need it. And we won't be paying anymore...we won't be paying Israel. We'll help Israel if they need it. They've been a great ally." The announcement could portend a significant shift in the U.S.-Israel relationship, which has long been underpinned by billions of dollars in American military assistance. Under a 10-year agreement signed during the Obama administration, the U.S. committed to providing Israel with $38 billion in military aid between 2019 and 2028. The earlier time frame raises questions about how the administration intends to suddenly halt the assistance, and whether Congress would need to approve the change. More than 90 percent of the money is directed to American defense companies, essentially never leaving the U.S. The Pentagon referred questions to the White House, which did not respond to a request for comment. The Israeli embassy could not be reached for comment. Trump, in the interview on Tuesday morning, said the annual assistance to Israel is a "bad talking point" for Democrats, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. "The left uses the $4 billion payment … as a signal of unfairness. And we can't allow that to happen. I don't like that. … It's almost too easy to target." Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.), who unsuccessfully pushed to cut military assistance to Israel while in Congress, suggested the announcement was motivated by Republicans' political troubles ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections. "Amazing how being on the verge of Republicans getting wiped out in the midterms changes hearts and minds," Greene wrote on social media. "Trump getting permission from Netanyahu to end annual aid to Israel isn't going to change today's election results. But it does show you how bad the polling is on that issue." The announcement also comes just a week after Israel's parliamentary elections left Netanyahu fighting to hold onto power. His Likud party emerged with the most seats, but his right-wing coalition fell short of the 61 seats needed for a majority, teeing up difficult negotiations to form a new government. Israel's standing in the United States has eroded over the past three years amid public outrage over the country's actions in the Gaza war. Many Democrats increasingly favor conditioning if not outright ending U.S military aid to Israel. A growing number of Republicans, eager to reduce U.S. military interventions abroad, see Israel as an obstacle to that goal. Israel is categorized as a major non-NATO ally, a designation which prioritizes it for arms sales and transfers of excess American military equipment. The vast majority of the military funding comes in the form of financing that allows Israel to buy U.S. military equipment. It traditionally includes $3.3 billion in foreign military financing and another $500 million for cooperative missile defense programs. The funding counts for less than one percent of the annual U.S. federal budget. Netanyahu has hinted for years that Israel will have to become more independent of U.S. military financing. He told CBS News earlier this year that he wanted to reduce U.S. support to zero. Trump insisted the Israeli leader first broached the topic. Netanyahu said, '"It would be appropriate if we don't receive aid,' because he understands that this is one of their points of contention." But Netanyahu is also keen to maintain U.S.-Israeli defense cooperation, especially on technology. Some in Israeli and American circles want to push for more such partnerships. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-says-end-billions-dollars-152022589.html

item.title: An unlikely player in the Michigan Senate race: Haley Stevens's fiancé
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Months before the high-stakes Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, Jason Turkish took such a hands-on role in Rep. Haley Stevens's campaign that her senior staff called a meeting without her to devise how to restrict his role, according to multiple people familiar with the meeting. Turkish was seen as relatively new to Stevens's orbit. Most of the congresswoman's senior staff knew him as a top donor some had met earlier in the campaign, which launched in 2025. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. By early June, Stevens and Turkish were said to be secretly engaged, according to multiple former campaign staffers who said the one-time donor had become Stevens's most important adviser. Stevens soon added him to private campaign text chains, one of the reasons staff called a meeting to figure out how to curtail his interactions with the team, according to one of the people familiar with the meeting. Tensions between staffers and a candidate's spouse or significant other are not uncommon in a campaign's intense atmosphere. They tend to erupt in crisis moments, and Stevens was facing tough polling in her race with Abdul El-Sayed. Now questions about Turkish's role in Stevens's primary campaign have been revived in the general election's closing hours, after the Democratic congresswoman's 11th-hour reversal of support for El-Sayed, the progressive Democrat who won the primary. This account is based on interviews with more than a dozen former Stevens campaign aides and other people familiar with the campaign. Stevens, 43, said that "any campaign staff being directly quoted in this article, I was made miserable by working with them." Asked whether she felt her campaign staff was trying to push out Turkish or limit his influence in any way, Stevens said, "I have nothing else to say about the campaign at this time." Turkish, a 39-year-old disability lawyer and political fundraiser, would not comment on whether staff sought to curtail his role, but he provided to The Washington Post emails from June and July showing that staff continued to reach out and consult him on campaign matters. He declined to address specific claims by former campaign staff on the record. "I was Haley Stevens's energetic and passionate supporter from the very launch of this campaign," he said. "And while the campaign ended in defeat, it also ended in our marriage. And along the path of that campaign, we spent thousands of hours together and around a campaign. And there were good days and bad days, but we lived it together, and we wouldn't trade it for anything." Turkish lives in Huntington Woods, a suburb north of Detroit, and works in Southfield as a managing partner at Nyman Turkish, a litigation and disability law firm. The Detroit News reported that the two met after Stevens's 2022 reelection campaign through David Kramer, a mutual friend. Stevens initially backed El-Sayed after their bruising primary, even telling people he was a "great candidate," but over the course of the general election, her public support for the candidate grew more strained, particularly as it related to El-Sayed's stance on Israel's war with Hamas, where he has become a leading voice denouncing U.S. support in what he labels a "genocide." Turkish endorsed El-Sayed's opponent in the key Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers, days before Stevens shocked the political world by backing Rogers and appearing with him at church on Sunday with Turkish. In an interview revealing his choice, he told the Detroit News that he saw an "escalation" in the Democratic nominee's rhetoric around Israel. Stevens's endorsement has led some close to her to express concern about Turkish's influence on her decision, including longtime friends, one who spoke with her as recently as Saturday night, mere hours before she backed Rogers on Sunday. The endorsement has effectively led Stevens to be excommunicated from her state's party, with the head of the Michigan Democratic Party writing that she was "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." Stevens said "any suppositions that Jason Turkish influenced me on Israel or campaign positions is absurd." Late Monday night, Stevens posted a lengthy explanation for her decision on X that lamented how "some critics have also dragged my fiancé into this, suggesting he or others must have made my decision for me." "Think about what that says. A woman can serve in Congress, run statewide, and fight for her convictions, and still be told that when she makes a choice people dislike, someone else must be pulling the strings," she wrote. "That is sexism dressed up as political analysis." One friend who spoke with Stevens said the congresswoman reassured her Saturday night that she would "never" rescind her endorsement of El-Sayed. "That primary was particularly brutal. For all involved," the friend said. "I feel that there is like an allegiance to him because he was there for her during a particularly dark and stressful time." But one aide said Stevens trusted Turkish and often valued his insight, particularly on Israel, because she agreed with him more than with her advisers, who were pushing her to be less supportive of Israel. After her endorsement of Rogers, many Israel supporters have applauded both Stevens and Turkish for what they view as a tough, gutsy stance. "By the time I got to the place where I was ready to do it, I would have been living a lie to a lot of people and in community. ... There was no way to circle the square," Stevens told the Detroit News on Monday. Stevens's senior staff first grew troubled by Turkish's campaign influence around June, people familiar with the campaign said. According to multiple people familiar with the exchanges, Turkish started berating staff for their work, particularly perplexed that he, a Stevens supporter, was being served digital ads about the campaign. He wanted more spent on digital fundraising, and he summoned a senior digital campaign staffer to his law office and yelled at her over the kind of digital content and fundraising emails the campaign was creating, the people said. He told a press aide that she was "not serving Haley well," two people familiar with the conversation recalled. Turkish would also send the congresswoman a list of hurtful tweets people were writing about her, four people familiar with Turkish's influence on Stevens said. Campaign staff also worried that when Turkish was the last person to speak with Stevens before an interview or event, she would stray from the campaign's talking points, the people said. "He was not a calming presence, in a way that in hindsight should have been more alarming," said Caitlin Legacki, a former top adviser to Stevens's campaign. "It was very strange. I have never seen anything like it." One former Stevens aide said campaign staff worked to prevent Turkish from showing up to events because of how he undermined staff. If he arrived, the person said, they would redirect cameras or reposition Stevens so that he could not draw the attention of the press. Before events, they said he often suggested rewriting talking points and insisted on joining Stevens's briefings before media appearances. The team tried to control his influence with two guardrails, multiple people said: Making sure he was not the last person to speak with Stevens before a public-facing event, and outlining how he was only allowed to go directly through the campaign's manager, Sam Barrett, not directly to lower-level staff, according to multiple sources familiar with the guardrails. "It did not work in the sense that he had any less influence on Haley," said Legacki, who left the campaign after it became public she was also working for the tech company Palantir while advising the campaign. Stevens said in an interview for this article that Legacki "was fired" because "of undisclosed conflicts." The changes meant Stevens's schedule was sometimes altered to ensure she spoke with a campaign staffer, and no one else, before certain events or calls, the people said. "We would organize the schedule to make sure there was a staff member who would be the last person talking to her because she did an interview or a donor call," said a person familiar with the campaign. Longtime friends say the couple grew even closer after her defeat. The morning after Stevens's primary loss to El-Sayed - a closer result than the polls anticipated - former Michigan governor James Blanchard (D) called her, thinking she would need some consoling, he said. Instead, she sounded ebullient. "I'm getting married!" she told Blanchard. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/unlikely-player-contentious-michigan-senate-134329642.html

The Justice Department in recent days has continued moving at an aggressive clip in ramping up its criminal investigation into the Alaska U.S. Senate race, sources familiar with the matter tell ABC News, with prosecutors in the process of issuing more than 100 subpoenas and at least twenty target letters and preservation notices alerting individuals they are targets of the probe. The investigation began accelerating last week after The New York Times detailed alleged efforts by Democrats and some in Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, to be on the ballot with incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan. "No one should be surprised that President Trump's Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day," Elias said in a statement. "This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President's political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets. Dan Sullivan gives a thumbs up to passing vehicles as he campaigns along a roadside on Election Day during the midterm elections in, Anchorage, Alaska, November 3, 2026. A DOJ spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News. item.title: Tennessee murderer captured in Missouri after prison escape and truck theft
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Authorities have captured a convicted murderer who evaded law enforcement for more than a week after escaping from a Tennessee prison. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation announced Tuesday that Jacob Morley was back in custody. He was arrested near Kansas City, Missouri, investigators said. "Thank you to the public for your assistance, vigilance, and the tips provided during this investigation," the bureau said in a statement. "We also thank all of our law enforcement partners for their continued efforts to safely bring this search to a successful conclusion." Missouri State Highway Patrol said it handled Morley's arrest alongside multiple partner agencies, after Tennessee authorities reported that Morley may be traveling through Missouri, based on footage obtained through Flock cameras. The arrest at around 11:30 a.m. local time near Norbone, a small city about an hour's drive from Kansas City, the state agency said. Little information about the inmate's escape, and the multi-state search for him, have been made available since Morley broke out of prison. But investigators said more will be released as it becomes available. Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence at the Northwest Correctional Complex in an isolated part of Tiptonville, a town roughly 90 miles from Memphis in northwestern Tennessee. He had been convicted of killing a coworker four years ago, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction. Correctional officers discovered Morley was missing from the prison at around 11:30 p.m. local time on Oct. 25, the department said. While parsing security cameras later on, investigators said they saw footage of Morley escaping the complex, while wearing his prison uniform, by slipping through a fence on the property. Authorities released additional security footage two days later that showed the inmate stealing a white 2008 Ford F-350, with Tennessee plates and a logo for Lindamood Planting Company on the side door, in the early hours of Oct. 27. It was stolen from Lake County, which includes Tiptonville, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said. The truck was located later the same day in Marion, Illinois, which is about 150 miles north of Tiptonville, the investigative bureau said . Morley's whereabouts were unknown at the time. The bureau had said earlier in the week that Morley was on its "most wanted" list, as various agencies, including the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, the governor's office and U.S. Marshals, offered combined rewards of up to $17,500 for information leading to his arrest. Investigators haven't shared details about how exactly the inmate escaped, beyond the fact that he breached a fence at the prison. Morley received a lifetime prison sentence for murdering Cody Birchfield, his former coworker, in 2022. Authorities said Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's home in Tennessee's Carter County after he had been missing for several weeks. In addition to first-degree murder, Morley was convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest, as he fled when deputies arrived at his home in 2022. Authorities said the manhunt for him at the time ended in North Carolina. Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold 1,776 inmates under varying degrees of security, from the lowest level up to maximum, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction. It also houses minors who have been convicted of crimes as adults. Multiple violent incidents have taken place inside the prison in recent years, some of which involved attacks between inmates and prison staff. In July, a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over the murders of five inmates, assaults against staff and other acts of violence. At a recent meeting of the Tennessee Inmate Disciplinary Oversight Board, members discussed ongoing problems in the prison and suggested issues with leadership played a role. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jacob-morley-escaped-tennessee-murderer-captured/

item.title: Prediction markets vs. polls: Election forecasting industry faces midterm test
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Prediction markets and pollsters both say Democrats are favored to take both the US House and Senate in the midterms. Prediction markets have been a little less certain about it, though traders’ odds jumped on Tuesday on the chances of Democrats taking control of the Senate. That's setting up what could be another chapter in the burgeoning rivalry between prediction markets and polls following 2024's closely watched results. The differences have been most evident in the upper chamber. A small but consistent gap has been evident for months in the odds of Democrats winning control of the Senate. The gap has averaged about 7.3 percentage points since Sept. 1, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis. But the gap has narrowed approaching Election Day, closing to 2.9 percentage points on Tuesday morning. Three prediction markets place a 77.3% chance of Democrats taking control, while two polling-based models put the chances a bit higher at 80.2%. The odds have been a bit more evenly matched around the House of Representatives, with an average gap of less than a percentage point in recent months. The latest read on Tuesday showed a 2.2-percentage-point gap, with prediction markets suggesting a 94% chance of Democrats flipping the chamber, versus 96.2% odds from polls. This analysis was conducted by averaging the daily odds from three leading prediction markets, Kalshi, Polymarket, and PredictIt, to create one rolling prediction market measure. Those values were then compared to the average of two leading poll-focused models — one from statistician Nate Silver and another from Harvard called ElectIt. These gaps have had an outsized effect on public perceptions in recent years. This was especially true in 2024, when a 10-percentage-point difference between prediction markets and polls led to some post-election analyses claiming that prediction markets had gotten the results right and polls had gotten them wrong. The stakes for prediction market companies are high. Kalshi and Polymarket have long argued that their markets are more truthful than polls because market participants have money on the line. The markets also had a high-profile miss recently when the winner of Brazil's presidential election was given just 20% odds before ultimately prevailing. The scrutiny also comes as these markets continue to grow rapidly. Kalshi shared new data over the weekend that more than $1.2 billion has now been traded on midterm markets, surpassing the platform's volume during the 2024 presidential election. Increased government scrutiny of the prediction markets Policymakers, meanwhile, have ramped up criticism of the sector and promised challenges on both the legislative and legal fronts. Senator Elizabeth Warren, who could lead the Senate's powerful banking committee if Democrats take power, and Republican Senator John Curtis teamed up on a recent letter to both Kalshi and Polymarket raising concerns about election-related prediction markets and possible market manipulation. "We are particularly troubled by election-related event contracts," the senators wrote. "Event contracts tied to elections receive prominent coverage and are treated by some observers as indicators of political momentum." A screen displays a Kalshi advertisement for a political markets in New York City on October 27. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon) Reuters / REUTERS In Curtis's home state of Utah, a lawsuit brought by Kalshi is challenging whether federal rules can overrule Utah's anti-gambling laws, which lawmakers want to apply to prediction markets. In an amicus brief supporting Utah, the group Better Markets wrote, "the stakes couldn't be higher ... Utah has every right to decide that Utahns shouldn't be subjected to sports betting's harms." A gap that proved significant in 2024 There are also echoes this year of the polling and prediction market situation on the eve of the 2024 election. Prediction markets gave Donald Trump better odds of winning and then capitalized when he prevailed. But the actual odds in the days before the election differed only in a matter of degree. The day before the election, prediction markets gave Trump between a 57% and 62% chance of victory. Many polls, meanwhile, showed the election as a dead heat, with Nate Silver writing on election morning in 2024 that Kamala Harris had a 50.015% chance of winning based on an average of dozens of polls. Yet the difference between those odds isn't as dramatic as it might seem. 50% odds imply that one side is likely to win 5 times if the election were held 10 times. 60% odds make it 6 out of 10. A Polymarket exhibit showed data relating to potential political candidates popularity on March 20, 2026 in Washington. (Alex Kent/The Washington Post via Getty Images) The Washington Post via Getty Images The prediction markets also underestimated the eventual winner in some respects, with Trump's odds of winning the popular vote listed at between 20-30% on Kalshi and Polymarket on election morning in 2024 before Trump did just that. But it didn't slow executives' victory lap. Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan argued that both higher odds in the days before the election as well as earlier movement on election night showed how they had "called the election." This story has been updated. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/prediction-markets-vs-polls-election-forecasting-industry-faces-midterm-test-100000463.html

item.title: Ballot counting issues reported in key New York swing district
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Election Day is here. Today, voters across the United States are heading to the polls to cast their ballots in the 2026 midterms . And with control of Congress up for grabs, the stakes are high for both parties as President Trump heads into his final two years in office. Democrats are seeking to regain control of both the House and Senate, while Republicans, who have held narrow majorities in both chambers since January 2025, are seeking to retain control. In the House, there are 435 seats. And while all of them are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% (or about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. The GOP currently holds 218 seats, compared with 214 held by Democrats. One seat is occupied by an independent (Rep. Kevin Kiley of California), and there are two vacancies (seats formerly held by GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas and Democratic Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick of Florida, who each resigned). To retake control of the House , Democrats would need a net gain of three seats. In the Senate, there are 100 seats, with 35 up for grabs and 12 or so considered competitive . Republicans currently hold 53 seats compared with 45 held by Democrats. There are two independents — Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine — who caucus with the Democrats. To wrest back control of the Senate, Democrats would need a net gain of four seats. To maintain Senate control, Republicans could still lose a net of three seats, since a 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote. There are also 36 gubernatorial races and numerous ballot measures to keep an eye on. Trump, whose approval ratings are at or near all-time lows, has spent the last month campaigning in battleground states, urging voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot to encourage higher turnout in hopes that it'll help Republicans avert a so-called blue wave . Some members of the GOP, however, appear to be bracing for one. "It could be quite a brutal evening," one senior GOP official told Politico . "Once the dominoes start falling, it becomes hard to stop them." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/live/midterms-2026-live-updates-election-day-voters-head-to-the-polls-as-democrats-look-to-flip-gop-control-of-the-house-and-senate-110000715.html

item.title: Midterms may bring in wave of historic firsts across U.S.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Featuring one of the most diverse slates of both Democratic and Republican candidates in recent years, this midterm election has set up a possible wave of historic leadership firsts across the country. Voters on Tuesday could propel into office the first Native American female governor and Native women senators, the first Black female governor, the first openly gay U.S. senator and the first Muslim U.S. senator , among other milestones. Most are Democrats, but the GOP could also break ground. While some of these candidates have avoided focusing on the inherent historic value of their race, gender, religion or sexual orientation, some voters' rights advocates are celebrating how the electorate has expanded. "These firsts show how our country is changing," Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity in democracy, said via e-mail. "For years, people of color and LGBTQ+ communities have organized, knocked on doors, talked to voters, held conversations, and done the hard work of saving our democracy," Anderson-Reed said. "These wins are because of them." Here are some of the races where history could be made. First Native American female governor Democrat Deb Haaland already broke barriers in 2018 as one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress. Then she became the first Native American cabinet secretary, running President Joe Biden's Department of the Interior. Charles Curtis, from the Kaw Nation, was President Herbert Hoover's vice president. Now the Laguna Pueblo citizen is poised to add first Native American woman governor to the list if she beats Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor, in New Mexico. Oklahoma is the only state to elect a tribal citizen for governor — Democrat Johnston Murray in the 1950s and current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt. Haaland shrugged off a question about her various political identities in a recent interview with The Associated Press. "I mean, somebody has to be the first," she said. "I just don't want to be the last, right?" But she says she's proud to see how Indigenous people care about representation as other Native women run. "It truly does matter," Haaland said. "It's not just a slogan." First Native woman senators Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik and a Democrat, was considered a trailblazer in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. House of Representatives. Now the former congresswoman is trying to do the same in the Senate by unseating Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. The honor could also go to Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive Democrat and a citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe who faces Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter. And if Tafoya wins, she too would make history — as the first Republican of Latina heritage to sit in the U.S. Senate. First Black female governor Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth could end a 250-year streak without a Black woman serving as a state's governor. Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, is running against Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman, to be governor of Georgia. If she wins, Bottoms would also be Georgia's first governor of color. All 83 of Georgia's previous governors have been white men. Demuth, the former Minnesota House speaker, is going up against longtime Minnesota U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar. Whatever the outcome, Minnesota will get its first female governor. Stacey Abrams is the only Black woman to come close to winning a governor's race when she got the Georgia Democratic Party's nomination in 2018 and 2022. First Muslim U.S. senator Abdul El-Sayed could be the first Muslim American to serve in the U.S. Senate. The progressive Michigan Democrat needs to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in what has been a very tight and contentious race. El-Sayed has had to contend with Republicans all the way up to Trump implying or overtly stating that the Michigan-born epidemiologist is not American and supports terrorism. Trump has called him "dangerously radical," "too extreme" and referred to him as "Mohammed." El-Sayed and his supporters have denounced the attacks as Islamophobic or racist affronts to religious freedom. First openly gay U.S. senator Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas could be the country's first openly gay senator if he's elected in New Hampshire. He is running against former Republican U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu. Pappas already became the first openly gay member of Congress when he was elected in 2018. This potential new benchmark is not something Pappas has dwelled on while campaigning, saying "I'm not running to make history." But he also applauded the fact that his sexual orientation was not a huge source of discussion among potential voters. First Black governors The U.S. could go from having only three elected Black governors in its 250-year history to gaining seven more overnight. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the third one in the U.S. and the only current Black governor, is projected to win re-election. Besides Georgia and Minnesota, he could also have new peers in Florida, Wisconsin, Nevada, South Carolina and Michigan. Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, has called the presence of so many Black gubernatorial contenders "a unique moment." It's not "an applause line" but a challenge to make diverse gubernatorial nominees more common, he said. Record year of women running for governor and Congress This midterm has been a record-breaker for women vying for state and federal offices. Democrats increased their 2022 number of women candidates to 19 running for governor, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. The Republican Party has seven women setting their sights on governor. Like Minnesota, Tennessee will elect its first female governor. The main candidates are Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn and Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilwoman. The election of the first Democratic Asian American woman as governor could happen in Vermont with Amanda Janoo, who is half Malaysian, or Oklahoma with Cyndi Munson, a former state lawmaker of Korean descent. Former Republican Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina, who is of Indian heritage, was the first Asian American female governor. Nearly 300 women, including incumbents, are running for the U.S. Senate and House, as documented by Rutgers' Center for American Women and Politics. Among them is Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois. If Stratton, who is Black, wins her Senate race, then she and fellow Democrat Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who is of Thai heritage, will make Illinois the first state to be represented by two female senators of color. ____ Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, and Savannah Peters in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/midterms-may-bring-wave-historic-200547667.html

item.title: NASA administrator defends 20-year-old Learjet co-pilot after Florida crash
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman took to his personal social media account Nov. 2 to defend the female co-pilot of the Learjet that crashed near Palm Beach, Florida. The private jet, bound from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, plummeted into the ground Nov. 1 near Greenacres and exploded into a fireball. All nine people onboard were killed. The cause of the crash was not immediately known, but heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time the jet went down, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement. Moments before the crash, a person in the cockpit said the crew was "managing the ice," encountering "moderate" turbulence and seeking "better rides," according to audio posted by LiveATC, a website that broadcasts air traffic control communications. That dramatic audio led to significant online criticism of the 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras, from Boca Raton. The pilot has not been identified. “Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts,” Isaacman wrote on X. “Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories. God bless them and their loved ones.” Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from… — Jared Isaacman (@rookisaacman) November 2, 2026 NASA Administrator defends Learjet copilot “Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman’s final radio calls,” Isaacman wrote. Isaacman is an experienced jet pilot and commercial astronaut. He bankrolled and organized two orbital spaceflights with SpaceX. Both included women onboard, and his first, Inspiration4, featured a female pilot , Sian Proctor. The NASA administrator went on to state that Filgueiras remained professional throughout the situation, knowing her life was about to end. She communicated with air traffic control right up until the crash. "She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," he wrote. “I understand the public interest given the footage and audio. But you do not know the aircraft’s maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit,” Isaacman wrote. The leaked cockpit communication with air traffic control revealed that the crew saw ice and experienced turbulence before the crash occurred. Isaacman said that it is common for charter companies, which fly these small jets, to hire fairly new commercial pilots and enable them to gain experience before many become commercial pilots. Filgueiras would have likely had all the applicable training, requirements, and checkouts required from the Federal Aviation Administration, he wrote. Evidence suggests the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas Chapman said at a Monday news conference. Brooke Edwards is a Space Reporter for Florida Today. Contact her at bedwards@floridatoday.com or on X: @brookeofstars .
